lessons.title: Describing village life
lessons.objective: Describe life in the village with clear, connected sentences.
lessons.course:
To describe, we say what we see, hear and do. We use describing words and linking words: first, then, also, in the evening.
Village life: people farm, fetch water from the stream, meet at the market on market day, sit together in the evening and tell stories.

support.title: Useful words
support.text: farm, stream, market day, compound, palm trees, quiet, busy, in the evening

lessons.model: “In my grandfather’s village, people wake up early and go to the farm. In the afternoon, children fetch water from the stream. On market day, the village is busy and noisy.”
lessons.guided: Look at a picture of a village. Say four sentences about it using first, then, also and in the evening.
lessons.exercise: Say one thing people do in the village in the morning.
lessons.answer: For example: they go to the farm.
lessons.remediation: Describe a picture with “I see …” sentences before linking them.
lessons.transfer: Describe your village or your quarter to someone in four sentences.

practice.prompt: Put the sentences in a good order.
items: Early in the morning, people go to the farm.
In the evening, families sit together.
practice.explanation: Linking words show the order.

practice.prompt: Which linking word shows that something comes after?
practice.explanation: “Then” shows what comes next.

practice.prompt: Listen to the description and say what happens on market day.
practice.listen: On market day, the village is busy. Women sell vegetables and men sell goats.
practice.answer: The village is busy; women sell vegetables and men sell goats.
practice.explanation: Listen for the words after “market day”.

lessons.title: Reading a description: the town market
lessons.objective: Read a short description silently and answer questions about it.
lessons.course: A description tells what a place or a person is like. We read it silently, picture it in our mind, then answer questions using words from the text.

support.title: Read silently
support.text: The market of Mbouda is big and colourful. At the entrance, a woman sells ripe pineapples. Further in, tailors sit at their sewing machines. Behind them, butchers cut meat on wooden tables. Everybody talks loudly, and motorbikes hoot outside.

lessons.model: The adult reads the text silently, then says: “I can see the pineapples at the entrance and the tailors further in.”
lessons.guided: Read the text silently. Draw a quick plan of the market: entrance, tailors, butchers.
lessons.exercise: What is sold at the entrance of the market?
lessons.remediation: Read the text aloud with the adult first, sentence by sentence.
lessons.transfer: Describe the market of your town in three sentences.
lessons.materials: The text; paper for the plan.

practice.prompt: Who sits at sewing machines?
practice.explanation: The text says tailors sit at their sewing machines.

practice.prompt: Put the places in the order of the text.
practice.explanation: The text goes from the entrance to the back.

practice.prompt: Find two words in the text that describe the market.
practice.explanation: Describing words tell what the market is like.

lessons.title: Spelling: the apostrophe ’s
lessons.objective: Use the apostrophe ’s to show that something belongs to one person.
lessons.course:
To show that something belongs to a person, we add ’s to the name or the noun: the chief’s palace, Mama’s pot, the teacher’s bag.
We write ’s only for owning, not for plurals: “two goats” has no apostrophe.
lessons.model: The adult writes: “the palace of the chief” → “the chief’s palace”; “the stall of Mrs Ewane” → “Mrs Ewane’s stall”.
lessons.guided: Turn five “of” phrases into ’s phrases. Check that no plural has an apostrophe.
lessons.exercise: Write with ’s: the house of Fon.
lessons.remediation: Use real objects: “This is Bih’s pen.”
lessons.transfer: Write three things that belong to people in your family with ’s.

practice.prompt: Complete with ’s.
practice.explanation: ’s shows that it belongs to one person.

practice.prompt: Which one is correct?
practice.explanation: A simple plural has no apostrophe.

practice.prompt: Write: the bicycle of my brother.
practice.explanation: brother + ’s.

lessons.title: Adjectives: common, proper and comparative
lessons.objective: Use common and proper adjectives and compare things with comparative adjectives.
lessons.course:
Adjectives describe nouns. Common adjectives: big, busy, old, quiet. Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and start with a capital letter: Cameroonian music, English books.
To compare two things we use the comparative: big → bigger, busy → busier, quiet → quieter. Long adjectives use more: more beautiful, more expensive. We add than: The town is busier than the village.
lessons.model: The adult compares two markets: “Douala market is bigger than Bafia market. The village is quieter than the town.”
lessons.guided: Compare pairs of pictures with comparative adjectives and than.
lessons.exercise: Complete: The town is ___ (noisy) than the village.
accept: The town is noisier than the village
lessons.remediation: Practise short adjectives with -er first (tall, small, big).
lessons.transfer: Compare two places you know in three sentences.
lessons.materials: Pairs of pictures (town and village, big and small objects).

practice.prompt: Complete with the comparative.
practice.text: A lorry is [[bigger]] (big) than a car. A city is [[busier]] (busy) than a village.
practice.explanation: big → bigger; busy → busier.

practice.prompt: Which one is a proper adjective?
practice.explanation: It comes from “Cameroon” and starts with a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Match each adjective with its opposite.
practice.explanation: Opposites help us describe and compare.

lessons.title: Comparing numbers: >, <, ≥ and ≤
lessons.objective: Compare numbers up to 500 with the symbols >, <, =, ≥ and ≤.
lessons.course:
> means “is greater than”: 340 > 290. < means “is less than”: 125 < 152. = means “is equal to”.
≥ means “is greater than or equal to”; ≤ means “is less than or equal to”. If a bus can carry at most 70 people, the number of passengers must be ≤ 70.
lessons.model: The adult compares the populations of two quarters: 425 > 398, because 4 hundreds is more than 3 hundreds.
lessons.guided: Compare pairs of number cards and place the right symbol between them.
lessons.remediation: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens.
lessons.transfer: Compare the prices of two things at the market.

practice.prompt: Which statement is true?
practice.explanation: Same hundreds; 0 tens is less than 5 tens.

practice.prompt: A taxi takes at most 5 passengers. Which numbers of passengers are allowed?
practice.explanation: At most 5 means less than or equal to 5.

practice.prompt: Match each symbol with its meaning.
pairs: is less than or equal to
practice.explanation: The open side faces the bigger number.

lessons.title: Adding numbers up to 500
lessons.objective: Add numbers up to 500 with and without carrying, and solve problems about the town.
lessons.course:
We write the numbers in columns: units under units, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. We add the units first. If the total is 10 or more, we carry 1 ten to the tens column.
  246
+ 138
= 384
lessons.model: The adult adds the passengers of two buses: 146 + 138. Units: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4, carry 1. Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2. Total: 284.
lessons.guided: Add three pairs of numbers in columns, saying aloud when you carry.
lessons.exercise: A shop sold 235 loaves on Monday and 148 on Tuesday. How many loaves in all?
lessons.transfer: Add the prices of two things you buy at the market.

practice.prompt: When do we carry?
choices: when a column adds up to 10 or more
practice.answer: when a column adds up to 10 or more
practice.explanation: 10 units make 1 ten.

lessons.title: Money: shopping up to 1 000 francs
lessons.objective: Recognise coins and notes up to 1 000 francs, pay and give change.
lessons.course:
We use coins of 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 and 500 francs, and notes of 500 and 1 000 francs.
To pay, we add the prices. To find the change, we subtract the bill from the money given: 1 000 − 650 = 350 francs change.
lessons.model: At the market, a bunch of plantains costs 600 frs and tomatoes cost 250 frs. Total: 850 frs. The adult pays 1 000 frs and gets 150 frs change.
lessons.guided: Play market with price labels and play money. Pay, then calculate the change.
lessons.exercise: You buy a book at 450 frs and pay with 500 frs. What is the change?
lessons.remediation: Use prices in hundreds only first.
lessons.transfer: Check the change when you buy something with an adult.

practice.prompt: Total of 350 frs and 425 frs?
Change from 1 000 frs for a bill of 725 frs?
Which coins make 600 frs?

lessons.title: Grid references on a town map
lessons.objective: Locate places on a simple map using grid references.
lessons.course:
A map can be divided into squares. Letters go across (A, B, C…) and numbers go up or down (1, 2, 3…). A grid reference gives the letter first, then the number: B3.
We use grid references to find places quickly.

support.title: Klassia town map (description)
support.text: A 3 × 3 grid. A1: market. B1: church. C1: bus station. A2: school. B2: town hall. C2: hospital. A3: football field. B3: post office. C3: police station.

lessons.model: The adult traces with a finger: “Go across to B, then down to 2: the town hall is in B2.”
lessons.guided: Draw a 3 × 3 grid of your quarter. Put five places in it and give their grid references.
lessons.transfer: Make a grid map of your house and its rooms.

practice.prompt: What is the grid reference of the hospital?
practice.explanation: Across to C, then to 2.

practice.prompt: Which place is in A3?
practice.explanation: A across, 3 down.

practice.prompt: Match each place with its grid reference.
practice.answer: market A1; town hall B2; post office B3.
practice.explanation: Letter first, then number.
